notes.heading: Define a biome
notes.body:
Biomes? 
In order to understand our world, geographers divide the planet up into distinct areas called biomes. 
Biomes
A large area of the Earth that is home to plant and animal communities with common characteristics which are adapted to that environment.

Biodiversity 
Amount of plants and animals in a biome. 
As you move away from the equator, biodiversity decreases. 
Tropical Rainforests have the greatest biodiversity in the world.

notes.heading: The nine biomes to learn
notes.body:
Polar Lands; Tundra; Boreal Forests; Mountain Vegetation; Temperate forest; Grasslands; deserts; Tropical forests; Aquatic.

The 10 Biomes of the World

1. Tropical Rainforest
2. Temperate Rainforest
3. Taiga (Boreal)
4. Tundra
5. Grasslands

6. Savanna Tropical Grasslands
7. Freshwater
8. Marine 
9. Ice 
10. Desert

notes.heading: Where biomes are: latitude, tropics, sub-tropics, temperate
notes.body:
What the study guide asks
- Know their latitudes.
- Using geographic language: latitude, tropics, sub-tropics, temperate describe where the world’s biomes are located.

Lines from the world maps (the 9 Food Security textbook maps)
- Arctic Circle, Tropic of Cancer, Equator, Tropic of Capricorn (north to south).

What your lessons say about where each biome is
- Tropical forests (palm oil case study): found mainly in tropical regions close to the equator.
- Grasslands / savanna: can be found in temperate, subtropical and tropical regions.
- Biodiversity: as you move away from the equator, biodiversity decreases. Tropical Rainforests have the greatest biodiversity in the world.
- Tundra: very low biodiversity.
- Boreal forest example: Finland Boreal Forest.
- Temperate rainforest example: Dandenong Ranges National Park, Victoria (cool temperate rainforest).
- Seagrass meadows (aquatic): ½ of the known 60 species are found in Australia’s tropical and temperate waters.

Australia’s biomes
- Map legend: Equatorial, Tropical, Sub Tropical, Desert, Grassland, Temperate.
- Tropical northern Australia: wetlands inhabited by First Nation Peoples for longer than 50,000 years.
- In the centre: a desert that is only 2nd to the Sahara (excluding Antarctica).
- In the South: temperate forests and grasslands dominate.

Using latitude in a description
- Satellite image of the Nile: 26° N latitude, 30° E longitude (well within the sub-tropics).

notes.heading: Climate, vegetation and animals of biomes
notes.body:
Biodiversity 
Amount of plants and animals in a biome. 
As you move away from the equator, biodiversity decreases. 
Tropical Rainforests have the greatest biodiversity in the world.

Tropical Deserts
Less than 250mm/year

Tropical Grasslands (Savanna) 
250mm-750mm/year

Finland Boreal Forest

Tundra
Very low biodiversity

Savanna Continued
Describe flat landscapes dominated by grass with few or no trees. 
Exist where rainfall is between 250mm and 900mm /year, enough rain for grass, not enough for forests. 
Can be found in temperate, subtropical and tropical regions.

Savanna in trouble? 
These environments are fragile and can quickly become deserts without proper management. 
Regular burning helps seeds germinate and prevents tree dominance. 
Grasslands provide essential habitat for native species.

Seagrass Meadows
Seagrasses are submerged flowering plants that form off long, sandy ocean beaches, creating dense areas that resemble meadows. 
Of the known 60 species of seagrass, ½ are found in Australia’s tropical and temperate waters. 
Provide habitats for sea turtles, lobsters etc. 
They: absorb nutrients from coastal run-off, slow water flow, help stabilize sediment and keep water clear

Are forests in its oldest growth stage. 
Old Growth Forests

Old Growth forest Benefits
Multi-layered, trees are of mixed ages. 
Generally few signs of human disturbance
Biologically diverse

Deserts

Australian deserts are places of temperature extremes. 
Daytime temps can exceed 50°C
Night time can drop to freezing 
Sand dominated: Simpson desert, Great Sandy Desert 
Smooth and Flat: Nullarbor Plain & Barkly Tableland 
Rocky and Hilly: Gibson Desert & Sturt Stony Desert

Climate
More than any factor, climate especially rainfall determines the type of farming practiced at a given location. 

Crops requiring lots of heat and water: 
 - Rice & Sugar Cane

Farming tolerating a wider range of temperatures: 
- Sheep & Camel farming

As a consequence, 
Farmers who share similar climate practice the same type of farming. 
This leads to large regions of the earth’s surface being farmed in the same way.

Technology
In some places, farmers are able to use technology to overcome the limitations of climate. 
In Australia, farmers use water from dams to irrigate their crops rather than relying on natural rainfall. 
Others, pump water from natural underground water storages called aquifers. 
Others use greenhouses to control temperatures and humidity to grow flowers and vegetables throughout the year.

notes.heading: Human damage to grasslands and environmental problems
notes.body:
European Occupation

Large scale Land clearing 
Irrigation of the land through water diversion from rivers and wetlands. 
New plant and animal species were introduced to the landscape
However, despite these changes Australia’s major biomes are still clearly evident.

Savanna in trouble? 
These environments are fragile and can quickly become deserts without proper management. 
Regular burning helps seeds germinate and prevents tree dominance. 
Grasslands provide essential habitat for native species.

Since European Settlement
Grasslands have primarily been used for grazing, reducing access to native wildlife.

Environmental Impacts of Irrigation



While irrigation has increased food production it has created major changes to biomes. 
It changes biomes by extracting water from rivers and lakes and the building of structures to store and transfer water.

Irrigation Water
Is applied to the land in much larger quantities than naturally occurs. 

This leads to changes in: 
soil composition
Waterlogging- the saturation of soil with ground water 
Salinity problems

Salinity

Overwatering of shallow rooted crops adds excess water to the water table causing it to rise. 

 Water table: the upper surface of groundwater in the soil or rock.
It is the level below the ground where all the spaces between soil and rock particles are completely filled with water.

Figure 4 (p. 420)     A Natural Forest


Large trees with deep root  systems. 
The roots drink the water, preventing the water table from rising.

Irrigation



Deep rooted trees have been cleared to make way for short rooted crops (such as corn or wheat) 
The crops cannot drink as much water as the large trees. 
The Water table rises.

Salinity After Irrigation 



The water table rises too much
It’s a combination of short water crops and too much irrigation. 
The water contains salt that kills plants 
Then erosion happens as there is no longer any roots left to hold the soil in place.

How to reverse salinity

Reduce irrigation volumes
Improve irrigation efficiency (e.g. drip instead of flood)

Other ways
Replant deep-rooted vegetation
Native trees and perennial plants:
Use more water year-round
Reduce groundwater recharge
Help lower the water table

Salt Tolerant Crops

Grow salt-tolerant crops
Barley
Saltbush- Used for livestock feed. 
Certain pasture species

What is soil? 
Many parts of the earth are covered in a thin fragile layer of soil. 
Plants grow in the soil to feed every animal on Earth (including you). 

Soil is a mixture of: 
Air
Water
Broken down rock
Organic material (tiny animals and plants)

As rocks break down into finer and finer particles….
The minerals within rocks become available to plants. 
Seeds carried onto weathered rock are able to germinate and send roots into the new soil. 
The plant dies and leaves fall onto the soil, they decompose and add fertility to the soil. 
This same process occurs with our compost bins. When you add apple cores, banana peels, they break down. 
Put that stuff onto your soil, plants love it.

Soil Layers
Over time, soil layers known as horizons form. 
They can be seen where a road has been cut through a hillside. 
By looking at soil horizons, farmers can tell how best to farm different areas. 
Top layer (O) Organic (this will look like brown leaves or compost)
2nd Layer (A) will look like dirt
3rd Layer (B) Will look like a mixture of dirt and rocks, lighter in colour
4th Layer (C) Will be mainly rocky, lighter in colour
5th Layer (Solid bedrock)

Australia
Australian soils are low in nutrients, thin and easily eroded. 
Australian farmers have adapted to this by adding fertilisers containing the nutrients plants need. 
As crops grow, they constantly draw nutrients from the soil so farmers must continue to replace them.

notes.heading: Cargo ships, containerisation and globalisation
notes.body:
Containerisation


Goods travel in standard-sized steel containers.
Cranes lift each container off the ship as one unit.
The same container fits on a truck trailer without unloading or repacking the goods.
Refrigerated containers keep perishable goods cold during the journey.

From ship to truck at the Port of Melbourne

A standard container moves as one unit, with the cargo still inside.

1   Ship to wharf
A crane lifts the whole container off the ship.


2   Terminal yard
The terminal can stack it until a truck is ready to collect it.


3   Truck to warehouse
Handling equipment lifts it onto a truck trailer. The truck takes it to a warehouse.

The time saving comes from moving one box. Workers can transfer hundreds of cartons in a single lift and unpack them at the warehouse.

How containerisation accelerated globalisation

Less handling at ports
Before containerisation, workers handled individual crates, sacks and barrels. A crane can now move an entire container in one lift.

Lower transport costs
Ships can spend less time at the wharf. Standard sizes let ports and trucks around the world handle the same box without repacking the goods.

More trade between countries
Cheaper, faster freight makes it easier for firms to buy parts overseas, manufacture in different countries and sell to customers around the world.

Trade Routes

Most of the product to and from Melbourne is from Singapore or Shanghai.

The Pilot: A specialist who drives the ships in 
Boards the vessel at the heads. 
Estimated takes 4 hours from the Heads to the port
Vessel Size: 350 m long, 48 m wide 
Able to carry 10,000 containers!

notes.heading: Drivers of globalisation and trade
notes.body:
Trade
Trade in the form of buying, selling of goods and services is s driving force that interconnects people all over the world. 
Trade has been going on since the beginning of human society. 
In contrast international trade is a modern phenomenon.

Trade
Can bring people together to share the Earth’s resources, but there can be problems when those resources are limited and potentially negative consequences for the environment.

9. 2 How does trade connect us? 
The Earth’s resources are not distributed evenly over space. 
Example some places have an abundance of iron ore and others may have none. 
To solve this problem, nations have developed trade, allowing producers and consumers to exchange goods and services. 
Pictured: An oil reserve map.

History of trade


Earliest form was as barter at local markets. 
Merchants also used land and sea routes to access foreign lands, where they exchanged goods for payment. 
More recently air has been used for trade and the internet to trade (Exchange information).

The Airbus A380
To construct this plane, component parts must be purchased from different countries and transported over land and sea to their final assembly in France.

Goods and Services
Are generated by either processing Earth’s resources (goods) or people doing services for others. 

Goods: Bread, motor car
Service: Something you can’t hold in your hand (education, doctor)

Transitions
The processing of a resource into more complex goods can be a series of transitions in which there is value adding (its value increases) at each level of industry. 
An important consideration in the production of goods and services is the environment.

4 Levels of Industry
1. Primary Industry- takes natural resources from the Earth or grows them. 
2. Secondary Industry- makes products from natural resources 
3. Tertiary industry- Sells products or services
4. Quaternary industry- Sells knowledge and information.

Australia’s Global Trade 

Australia is one of the 164 members of the World Trade Organization, which covers 95% of global trade. 
The organisation promotes free and fair trade between countries .
Since 2001, it has aimed to help the world’s poor by slashing tradie barriers (tariffs quotas and farm subsidies.) 

Trade barriers: A government imposed restriction (tariffs, quotas and subsidies )on the free international exchange of goods and services.

DFAT


The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFAT) coordinates trade agreements on behalf of the Australian government and promotes the export of goods and services. 

73.5% of our trade is with the Asia Pacific Economic Forum (APEC)

Imports 


Like many countries, Australia is not self-sufficient in all goods and services. 
Australia imported $395 billion of goods and services . 

1. Personal Travel 
2. Cars
3. Refined petroleum
4. Ships
5. Telecom Equipment and Parts
6. Computers

Food Trade Around the World


The world’s population is unevenly distributed across space, as is the quantity of food produced. 
Some places such as Australia, produce an abundance of food, while others struggle to produce enough to maintain food security.

The Flow of Food Trade
Much of the flow of food trade is controlled by powerful countries such as the: USA, China and international trade agreements. 
The WTO and the G20 (the most powerful 20 nations) Have a significant say in the flow of food products around the world, particularly with respect to tariffs and fair trade rules.

notes.heading: Tariffs, quotas and subsidies
notes.body:
What is International Trade?

Countries buy and sell goods and services.
• Trade links producers and consumers worldwide.
• Governments may restrict trade using barriers.

Trade Barriers

Trade barriers are policies that make international trade more difficult.
• Three common barriers: tariffs, quotas and subsidies.
• Used to protect local industries and jobs.

Tariffs

A tariff is a tax on imported goods.
• Imported products become more expensive.
• Can encourage consumers to buy local products.

Quota
A quota limits the quantity of a product that can be imported.
• Protects local producers from foreign competition.
• Can lead to higher prices for consumers.

Subsidies
A subsidy is money provided by the government to support businesses.
• Helps local industries lower costs.
• Can make domestic products more competitive.

Advantages of Trade Barriers

Protect local jobs.
• Support new industries.
• Reduce dependence on imports.

Disadvantages of Trade Barriers

Higher prices for consumers.
• Less choice of products.
• Possible trade disputes between countries.

notes.heading: Essay option — A specific threat to food security
notes.body:
Defining Food Security 

Very few Australians, by choice, would go to bed hungry. 
We live in a country where there is plentiful supply and a wide range of foods available. 
Food Security- having reliable access to enough nutritious food, whether that’s growing it or being able to afford it.

At a National Scale

For a country, food security means being able to:
 
Produce enough food
Ability to afford the food
Ability to Import food

Factors impacting food security in other regions 

Environmental Factors- Diverse climate zones, soil types, rainfall
Economic Factors- High production costs, export market, modern infrastructure
Technological Factors- Precision agriculture, advanced irrigation systems, research capabilities

Water Quality: Water Pollution


When water quality deteriorates, it creates a cycle. 

Crops don’t grow as well
Soil becomes less productive
Livestock can get sick
Food can become unsafe to eat.

Sources of water quality problems


Farming: 
Excess nutrients from fertilisers
Pesticides 
Soil Erosion can run off from farmlands into streams

Sources of Water Quality Continued


Cities:

1. Industrial waste
2. Untreated sewerage 
3. Urban Run-Off

The Salt Problem

Biggest challenges for Australian farmers is soil and water salinity. 
When irrigation systems aren’t properly managed, salt builds up in the soil .
The soil becomes too salty for farming. 
Seen in the Murray Darling Basin

Environmental Changes

1. Rising Sea Levels affecting coastlands
2. Different rainfall patterns affecting where crops grow
3. More extreme weather events like droughts and floods. 
4. New patterns of pests and plant diseases arise

How it affects the economy?

1. Farmers need money to adapt to new conditions 
2. Crop yields can go up or down. 
3. Insurance costs go up or down
4. Food prices become less predictable 
5. Farmer expertise no longer relevant

Challenges Farmers/Governments Face 

Which crops to grow as conditions change
How to protect threatened farmers areas 
Whether to help farmers adapt or relocate 
How to work with other countries on food security

The Australian Story 

Australian farmers already feeling the effect of climate change. 
The climate is becoming more unpredictable
Growing seasons are shifting, requiring changes to planting and harvest times 
New pests and diseases are emerging where they were previously unseen.

notes.heading: Essay option — A geographical feature and human interconnections
notes.body:
First Nations People
First Nations Australians do not view the land as just one solid thing; rather land represents three key interconnected elements of their world.

Physical, cultural and sacred worlds.

Physical
Land, rivers, mountains and skies

Cultural

This is the human system of knowledge and practice:
Language, kinship systems, laws, ceremonies
Storytelling, art, songlines, and traditions
Rules about how to behave and care for Country
Passes knowledge from one generation to the next
Teaches responsibilities (e.g. caring for land, respecting elders)Keeps communities strong and connected

Sacred
Ancestral beings who created the land and life
Sacred sites and stories tied to specific places
Ongoing spiritual presence in the landscape
Physical → what you can see and touch
Cultural → what people do and pass on
Sacred → the spiritual meaning behind everything

Hunters & Gatherers: The San
Or Kalahari Bushmen live in the Kalahari desert in Southern Africa. 
6% still live in the traditional way 
They roam in regions up to 1000 square miles. 
No pack animals and few possessions (only spears, arrows, bowls and water bags) 
Clothes made of animal skins
They are experts at finding water and tracking animals. 
Men hunt wildebeests and antelope
Women hunt lizards, frogs and tortoises and gather roots, berries

Nomadic Herders: The Bedouin 
Bedouin people are nomads that mainly live in Syria, Iraq, Jordan, the countries of the Arabian Peninsula and the Sahara. 
Some are camel herders or herd sheep and goats on the desert fringes. 
Bedouin communities rarely stay in a place longer than a week.
notes.caution: Evidence bank only. The desert example in the deck describes the San and Bedouin and their connections to place; do not add unsupported case-study statistics.

exams.title: Study-guide revision paper
exams.source: Year 9 Exam Study Guide.docx.txt; lesson sources shown per question; format: 2025 Test.docx.txt
exams.instructions: Independent revision paper, not an official school test. Section I: 5 marks. Section II: 29 marks. Section III: choose ONE of four responses for 16 marks. Total: 50. Question wording, mark allocations and practice rubrics are author-assigned; factual answers are drawn only from the named school files. Missing-map questions have not been fabricated.

questions.prompt: Which term describes plant and animal communities adapted to a large area?
questions.explanation: A large area of the Earth that is home to plant and animal communities with common characteristics which are adapted to that environment.

questions.prompt: Which trade barrier is a tax on imports?
questions.explanation: A tariff is a tax on imported goods.

questions.prompt: In the L6 lesson, what does the Q in PQE stand for?
questions.explanation: L6 lists Pattern, Quantify, Exception (and adds Substantial, as PQES). The earlier L1 Biomes slide writes the Q as Quantity.

questions.prompt: Which is listed as an advantage of palm oil?
questions.explanation: The slide lists contributes to the economy and provides jobs as pros.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT intensive farming?
questions.explanation: Wheat farming is not an example of intensive farming.

questions.prompt: Define a biome and list the nine biomes on the exam study guide.
questions.modelAnswer:
Definition: A large area of the Earth that is home to plant and animal communities with common characteristics which are adapted to that environment.
Nine biomes: Polar Lands, Tundra, Boreal Forests, Mountain Vegetation, Temperate forest, Grasslands, deserts, Tropical forests, Aquatic.
Suggested self-mark: definition 1; complete guide list 3.
questions.source: Year 9 Exam Study Guide.docx.txt; L1 Biomes.pptx.txt

questions.prompt: Describe the grassland landscape and rainfall described in the Australian-biomes lesson, then give a human use and an environmental concern.
questions.modelAnswer:
Flat landscapes dominated by grass with few or no trees; rainfall between 250mm and 900mm/year in this deck. Grasslands have primarily been used for grazing since European settlement. They are fragile and can become deserts without proper management.
Suggested self-mark: landscape 1; rainfall 1; grazing 1; fragility/desertification 1.

questions.prompt: List three advantages and three disadvantages of palm oil.
questions.modelAnswer:
Advantages: contributes to the economy; provides jobs (the two pros on the L4(2) Pros slide); useful as an ingredient in food, cosmetics and biofuel (from the L4(2) case-study slide, not listed as a pro).
Disadvantages: widespread deforestation; loss of biodiversity; human-rights/First Nations community issues.
Suggested self-mark: 1 for each source-backed point.

questions.prompt: Explain how containerisation has improved world trade and globalisation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Standard-sized steel containers are moved by crane as one unit. The same box fits a truck without unloading/repacking. Less handling saves time at the wharf and lowers transport costs. Cheaper, faster freight makes it easier to buy parts overseas, manufacture in different countries and sell around the world.
Suggested self-mark: standardisation 1; reduced handling/time 1; lower costs 1; international producer/consumer link 1.

questions.prompt: Explain two drivers of trade and define tariffs, quotas and subsidies.
questions.modelAnswer:
Resources are unevenly distributed, so trade lets producers and consumers exchange goods and services. Countries are not self-sufficient in all goods and services.
A tariff is a tax on imports; a quota limits imported quantities; a subsidy is government money supporting businesses, lowering local costs.
Suggested self-mark: two drivers 2; three barrier definitions 3.

questions.prompt: Choose salinity as a degradation process: explain a human cause, its effect on soil/plants, and a source-backed management response.
questions.modelAnswer:
Deep-rooted trees are cleared for shallow-rooted crops. Overwatering adds excess water to the water table, causing it to rise. Salty water kills plants; without roots to hold soil, erosion occurs. Reduce irrigation volumes, improve irrigation efficiency or replant deep-rooted vegetation.
Suggested self-mark: cause 1; process/impact 1; response 1.
questions.origin: Adapted from old Food-Security-Study/02-Practice-Exam.md, question 8; checked against L13 Salinity.pptx.txt

questions.prompt: What does each part of PQE stand for?
questions.modelAnswer:
Pattern; Quantify; Exception.
Suggested self-mark: 1 for each term. The source supplies the headings only, not an unseen map.

sections.title: Section III — Extended response
sections.instructions: Choose one prompt only. All four plans use source evidence; gaps in the supplied model material are labelled.

questions.prompt: Should rice farming be allowed in Australia?
questions.modelAnswer:
Source-backed plan / evidence bank (not a supplied model essay):
- Rice needs heat and water (L2 Climate).
- Dams and aquifers allow irrigation rather than reliance on rainfall (L2 Climate).
- Irrigation extracts water from rivers and lakes and changes biomes (L13).
- Shallow-rooted crops and excess irrigation can raise the water table; salty water kills plants and loss of roots promotes erosion (L13).
- Evaluate using lower irrigation volumes, efficient irrigation and deep-rooted vegetation as management evidence (L13).
No rice-specific production statistics or full essay are supplied.
Suggested practice rubric (author-assigned, not a school marking key): clear position 4; relevant source evidence 4; explanation of benefits/costs 4; supported judgement 4.
questions.source: Year 9 Exam Study Guide.docx.txt; L2 Climate.pptx.txt; L13 Salinity.pptx.txt

questions.prompt: Food security: discuss a specific example that threatens food security.
questions.modelAnswer:
Source-backed plan / marking points:
- Define food security using L1.
- Example: soil and water salinity in the Murray–Darling Basin (L3 (1), slide 14; booklet p.459).
- Explain irrigation mismanagement and salt build-up; soil and drainage water become too salty for farming (booklet).
- Link the crop/soil impact to food production.
- Management: reduce irrigation, improve efficiency, replant deep-rooted vegetation (L13).
Suggested practice rubric (author-assigned): definition/example 4; causal process 4; food-production consequences 4; evidence-based response/judgement 4.
questions.source: Year 9 Exam Study Guide.docx.txt; L1 (1).pptx.txt; L3 (1).pptx.txt; L13 Salinity.pptx.txt; 9 Food Security PDF.txt p.459

questions.prompt: Using an example, discuss a geographical feature that has influenced human interconnections.
questions.modelAnswer:
Source-backed plan / evidence bank:
- Use the desert environment example in L1(2).
- The San live in the Kalahari desert in Southern Africa; the lesson describes expertise in finding water/tracking animals, hunting and gathering.
- The Bedouin are described as nomads, with camel, sheep or goat herding on desert fringes.
- For connections to place, the deck distinguishes physical (land, rivers, mountains, skies), cultural (knowledge, kinship, laws, stories and responsibilities) and sacred elements.
No complete essay/marking key is supplied.
Suggested practice rubric (author-assigned): named feature/example 4; relevant source evidence 4; explanation of connections 4; supported discussion 4.

questions.prompt: Explain how the Port of Melbourne contributes to globalisation. Evaluate its economic and social importance for Victoria and Australia.
questions.modelAnswer:
Source-backed plan / evidence bank:
- Explain standard containers and the ship → terminal yard → truck → warehouse pathway.
- Less handling, less time at the wharf and lower freight costs facilitate overseas parts, multinational production and global customers.
- Use source examples of fuel, dry bulk, general cargo and vehicle terminals; Singapore and Shanghai are named trade links.
- The deck supplies mechanisms and goods but not a full social/economic evaluation or employment/GDP statistics. Do not invent totals.
Suggested practice rubric (author-assigned): globalisation explanation 4; port evidence 4; economic discussion 4; supported social/economic evaluation 4. The final component requires your own argument from the supplied examples, not a memorised invented model.
questions.source: Year 9 Exam Study Guide.docx.txt; Port of Melbourne Revised(1).pptx.txt

exams.title: 2023 test — text-only edition
exams.instructions: Original test: 24 marks. This text-only edition: 22 marks. Original Q4 (map values) and Q7 (graph) omitted because their figures are unavailable. Q1 and Q10 refer to a map that is not shown, but can be answered from the question text. Original question numbers retained. The source does not state a time limit; 50 minutes is an optional practice timer, not an original instruction.

questions.prompt: Original Q1. Rice is only considered a food staple in the Asian region. True or false?
questions.stimulus: The original refers to a world map of staple foods (Figure 1, data from FAO). The map is not available; the statement can be answered without it.
questions.explanation: Rice is also a staple food in parts of Africa, South America and the Middle East.

questions.prompt: Original Q2. Corn or maize is a common food staple and it can also be used as an animal food source and as a biofuel. True or false?
questions.explanation: Corn or maize is a common food staple and it can also be used as an animal food source and as a biofuel.

questions.prompt: Original Q3. The Green Revolution in agriculture was primarily to introduce people to a wider variety of green food crops such as green vegetables. True or false?
questions.explanation: The Green Revolution relates to rapid increases in agricultural productivity due to advancements in seed technology, the use of fertilisers to increase yields and better farm management.

questions.prompt: Original Q5. Traditional Indigenous Australians’ use of fire to manage their land and food resources was an unsustainable practice. True or false?
questions.explanation: Traditional Indigenous Australians used fire very carefully to manage their land and food resources. They planned to leave sufficient eggs, seeds and plants to allow for continual growth so that they could return to the same place and hunt and harvest again.

questions.prompt: Original Q6. Global food production has to increase to feed the growing world population. There are three main ways to achieve this growth. Which of the following is NOT one of these ways?
options: Increasing the area of land being used by converting natural habitats to farmland
Increased yield per unit area of land
Increasing the variety of crops grown
questions.explanation: Increasing the variety of crops grown is not one of the ways listed.

questions.prompt: Original Q8. Which would NOT be an example of intensive farming?
options: A vineyard (producing table and wine grapes)
questions.explanation: Wheat farming is not an example of intensive farming.
questions.stimulus: Intensive farming typically requires a large input of time, money and labour in the preparation and harvesting of food crops, and is usually practised over a fairly small space. Items are often perishable and need to be close to the markets.

questions.prompt: Original Q9. Ideal conditions for rice growing in South-East Asia are:
options: High temperatures in summer, low temperatures in winter, hillsides for terraces
High temperatures, low rainfall, steep slopes and large amounts of water available
Moderate temperatures, dry summers, fertile soils and steep slopes
High temperatures, flat land, fertile soil and large amounts of water available
questions.explanation: High temperatures, flat land, fertile soil and large amounts of water available.

questions.prompt: Original Q10. The type of farming practised in many places in Australia is directly related to the amount of water available. What are the main types of agriculture that can be practised in desert environments?
questions.stimulus: The original map, “Types of agriculture in Australia”, is not available; the options can be answered without it.
options: Extensive grazing of cattle for meat and sheep for wool
Intensive grazing of cattle for meat, and sheep for meat and wool
Cereal grains and cattle for milk
There are none; it is desert and therefore there can be no agriculture.
questions.explanation: The main types of agriculture that can be practised in desert environments are extensive grazing of cattle for meat and sheep for wool.

questions.prompt: Original Q11. Explain the difference between extensive and intensive farming, and provide examples of their types of produce.
questions.modelAnswer: Extensive farming is generally carried out on very large farms, often covering thousands of hectares. They may graze cattle and/or sheep for meat and wool, or grow crops such as wheat. Intensive farming is carried out on smaller properties, usually closer to the urban centres that they supply. Intensive farming produces items such as milk, fruit and vegetables.

questions.prompt: Original Q12. Greenhouses are capable of creating optimum growing conditions for plants. List three examples of features in the natural environment that can be controlled or changed within a greenhouse environment.
questions.modelAnswer: Answers may vary: temperature; rainfall/humidity; wind; soils (fertility and composition).

questions.prompt: Original Q13. Describe two ways in which the natural landscape can be modified to suit food production. Give examples where possible.
questions.modelAnswer: Answers may vary: cutting terraces for rice farming into hillsides; reclaiming land from the sea; ploughing to reduce small hills and create flat land; draining wetlands; applying fertilisers and other chemicals to improve soil structure and fertility.

questions.prompt: Original Q14. Irrigation is the artificial application of water to the land to improve farming. Describe three benefits that irrigation can bring to agriculture.
questions.modelAnswer: Answers may vary: supplements insufficient/unreliable rainfall; reduces risk/impact of drought; increases plant yields; allows a greater variety of crops; allows intensive cropping in areas previously only suitable for grazing.

questions.prompt: Original Q15. Outline two food-related issues faced by people living in remote communities in Australia.
questions.modelAnswer: Cost and availability of high-quality foods are issues faced by people living in remote communities. Long distances can cause high transport and storage costs. Access to a regular supply of fresh fruit, vegetables and dairy products can be difficult.

exams.title: 2025 test — text-only edition
exams.source: 2025 Test.docx.txt; 9 Food Security PDF.txt; 2023 Test.docx.txt (MCQ cross-check)
exams.instructions: Original paper: 50 marks / 50 minutes. This edition: 40 marks. Original Q1 (map, 1 mark) and Q6 (population graph, 8 marks) omitted because the figures are missing. Q3 (1 mark) omitted because the supplied text has no explicit answer key and the booklet does not establish all the alternatives. Q11 uses the source photo caption as a text description. Original section structure, question numbers and remaining marks retained. Other MCQ answers were cross-checked with the booklet or the 2023 test.

questions.prompt: Original Q2. Which areas of the world have the highest levels of food security?
questions.explanation: The test’s answer sheet gives no multiple-choice key. The booklet (lesson 10.2) describes Australia’s plentiful food supply and relatively high standard of living, which enables most people to afford food.

questions.prompt: Original Q4. What is the name given to the widespread changes between 1950 and 1980 to improve food security?
questions.explanation: The 2023 test identifies the Green Revolution with seed technology, fertilisers and improved farm management.

questions.prompt: Original Q5. A widespread shortage of food is known as:
questions.explanation: Booklet lesson 10.8: a famine is an extreme crisis of access to adequate food, resulting in widespread malnutrition and loss of life — the worst form of food insecurity.

questions.prompt: Original Q7. List the five main factors that are risks to food security.
questions.modelAnswer: Water scarcity; climate change; population growth; competition for land; land degradation.

questions.prompt: Original Q8. In your own words, define food accessibility.
questions.modelAnswer: Food accessibility means physical and economic access to food. It means there is enough food available and it is within reach of those who need it.

questions.prompt: Original Q9. What are some effects of changing productive farmland into tourism and recreation facilities?
questions.modelAnswer: While tourism income is reliable, recreation facilities can require high levels of water usage, affecting what is available for crop irrigation and other uses. Loss of agricultural land means a loss of food production capacity for the region. An increase in the number of people in a region places greater demands on resources in the area.

questions.prompt: Original Q10. Name four uses for water that might place a strain on the world's water supply.
questions.modelAnswer: 1 mark each for any four: domestic (drinking, washing, cooking); agriculture (food production, mainly irrigation); industry (manufacturing); recreation (leisure activities); environment (wetlands and forests).

questions.prompt: Original Q11. What would be a direct effect of rising sea levels caused by climate change? How does this relate to food security in this rice-growing region?
questions.modelAnswer: A small rise in sea level of a few centimetres would cover the crop in salty water, destroying it. This could lead to greater risks to food security in these rice-growing regions, threatening the lives of huge populations of people.
questions.stimulus: Text description supplied by the source in place of the photo: Rice seedlings in soil containing salt.

questions.prompt: Original Q12. Evaluate two views: the world's population is growing faster than farmers can feed it; or food production has kept pace with population growth. Give reasons for each.
questions.modelAnswer:
Answers will vary. View 1: rapid growth may bring food insecurity, starvation and famine; existing freshwater and soil resources are degraded; much population growth is in areas already at risk, such as parts of Africa.
View 2: food production has kept pace and sometimes exceeded population growth; technology improves yields; population growth shows signs of slowing; humans can adapt through research and innovation; genetic modification may increase productivity and yields.

questions.prompt: Original Q13. Why are there likely to be food shortages during periods of armed conflict in a region?
questions.modelAnswer:
Possible reasons from the supplied answer:
- Disruption of food markets and food aid
- Hunger used as a weapon of war
- Farmland repurposed
- Crops not planted or tended
- Irrigation systems and farming areas destroyed
- Water supplies targeted
- Animals and food confiscated to supply fighters
- Community members become soldiers and are unavailable to farm
- Aid delivery disrupted by fighting
